etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English respounden, from Old French respondre, from Late Latin respondō, from Latin respondeō. Cf. Modern French répondre.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To say something in return; to answer; to reply.
(intransitive) To act in return; to carry out an action or in return to a force or stimulus; to do something in response.

quote.citation: 2012 January, Robert M. Pringle, “How to Be Manipulative”, in American Scientist‎[1], volume 100, number 1, archived from the original on 3 October 2013, page 31:
quote.text: As in much of biology, the most satisfying truths in ecology derive from manipulative experimentation. Tinker with nature and quantify how it responds.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To correspond with; to suit.

quote.citation: 1600, [Torquato Tasso], “(please specify |book=1 to 20)”, in Edward Fairefax [i.e., Edward Fairfax], transl., Godfrey of Bulloigne, or The Recouerie of Ierusalem. […], London:  […]  Ar[nold] Hatfield, for I[saac] Iaggard and M[atthew] Lownes, →OCLC:
quote.text: For his great deeds respond his speeches great.

definitions.definition: A versicle or short anthem chanted at intervals during the reading of a lection.
(architecture) A half-pillar, pilaster, or any corresponding device engaged in a wall to receive the impost of an arch.
